newsitem.title: USA: Cooling brain hastens coma recovery - study.
newsitem.headline: Cooling brain hastens coma recovery - study.

text.p: Quickly cooling the body to a state of hypothermia after a severe brain injury can speed recovery from a coma, researchers report in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

Doctors at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre randomly assigned 82 patients with head injuries to receive regular treatment or have their bodies cooled to a core temperature of 90 degrees (32.2 Celsius) for 24 hours. The cooling process began within six hours after the injury.

They found that one year later 62 percent of the patients whose bodies were cooled had been able to return to independent living, compared to 38 percent of the patients who received standard care, which involves reducing brain swelling. The induced hypothermia technique worked best among head injury victims who had not fallen into the deepest levels of coma.

The findings by Dr. Donald Marion and his Pittsburgh colleagues confirm an observation made in 1943 that hypothermia seems to protect the brain as it tries to recover from serious trauma. Cooling helps relieve pressure in the brain.

Many questions about the technique had remained unanswered, such as how long and how much to cool a body and how much time can pass after the injury before any cooling becomes useless. The new study was an attempt to resolve some of those questions.

The Marion team cooled their patients using special blankets and a tube that circulated ice water in the stomach. After the body's core temperature reached 90 degrees, the patient was kept cold for 24 hours. It took another 12 hours to return the body to its normal temperature of 98.6 (37 Celsius). Hypothermia sets in when body temperature falls below 95 degrees (35 Celsius).

All 82 patients received drugs to prevent shivering. Three months after their injury, 38 percent of the patients whose bodies had been cooled had come out of the coma and were capable of caring for themselves. The rate was 17 percent for people whose bodies were kept warm.

At the 12 month mark, the hypothermia group was also doing significantly better. Marion and his colleagues found, however, that not all comatose patients did equally well. For those in the deeper levels of coma, who rated a 3 or 4 on the Glasgow Coma Scale, hypothermia had no effect.

When the coma was less deep and the rate on the coma scale ranged from 5 to 7, 73 percent of the patients whose bodies had been cooled suffered no permanent disability or were at least well enough to care for themselves, versus 35 percent of the people in the other group.
The study was financed by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
